While biology is the study of living organisms, mathematical biology is the application of mathematical tools to give enhanced understanding of biological systems. In particular, we will study equations that capture the key features of a given system. Constructing such models requires stripping away the systems complex nature and identifying a handfull of key quantities required to describe how the system changes. 

The key quantities we consider broadly fall into two categories: fixed quantities that do not change in time, called **constants**, and quantities that evolve in time, called **dynamical variables**. Quantities whose values are specified a priori are called **parameters**, and are typically constant in time (though can be dynamic with clear defined behaviour), while quantities whose values are determined by the model are called **variables** or **degrees of freedom**.

When we say that a quantity changes in time, an important consideration is whether time is modeled as continuous, $t \in \mathbb{R}^{+}$, such that changes occur infinitesimally, or discrete, $t \in \mathbb{Z}$, such that changes occur in finite steps (e.g., yearly updates).

## Population Dynamics

A key problem in biology is modelling mathematically how the population of various species changes over time (tracking births, deaths and migration). This might be quite abstract when studying, for example, the population of a chemical. As with our general approach we must identify the salient dynamical degrees of freedom (variables that change over time), the most obvious of which is,
$$
N(t) - \text{Population change as a function of time},
$$ {#eq-noLabel}

though there may be other variables involved or multiple competing populations.

## Exponential Growth

If we assume the simplest population model with fixed birth rate and death rate, then every member of the species has the same fixed probability of giving birth and dying. For a change in time $\Delta t$ the number of births is $b\,\Delta t$ and the number of total deaths is $d\, \Delta t$, where we call $b$ the **birth rate** and $d$ the **death rate**, such that,

$$
N(t + \Delta t) = N(t) + (b - d)N(t)\Delta t.
$$ {#eq-exponential}

If $\Delta t$ is finite then this is a discrete exponential model (called the Malthusian model) and if it is infinitesimal $\Delta t \rightarrow 0$ then we have the first order continous differential equation,

$$
\frac{dN}{dt} = (b-d)N = rN.
$$ {#eq-continousExp}
For convenience we will define the constant $r = b-d$. The solution follows from previous courses on ODEs,

$$
N = N_0 \, e^{rt}
$$ {#eq-expSol}

where $N_0$ is the initial population at time $t=0$. Note that this model predicts that population grows or shrinks (depending on the sign of $r$) indefinitely. Unsurprisingly such a simplistic model is rarely accurate. 

It is important to note that in everyday language the word exponential is often used not to refer to a system with such behaviour, for example you will have no doubt heard people refer to the exponential growth of the world population, which can be seen in @fig-worldPopulation. For most of our history (until the 1960's) we have experienced super-exponential growth (where the exponent $r$ increases with time) and since then $r$ has started to decrease. It is even predicted that the exponent may become negative in the future leading to population decrease.

![World population taken from [our world in data](https://ourworldindata.org/population-growth-over-time). Population to date is in dark green and predicted trends in light green, including the associated annual change in red. Note, a constant red line would correspond to exponential growth.](images/worldPopulation.png){#fig-worldPopulation}

## Logistic Equation and Population Caps

To modify the above simplistic approach we might consider a variable birth and death rate that depends on population,


\begin{align}
N_{t+1} = \left( b(N_t) - d(N_t) \right) N_t & - \text{Discrete model,}\\
\frac{dN}{dt} = \left( b(N) - d(N) \right) N & - \text{Continous model,}
\end{align}

which is hardly a model without understanding how the general functions $b(N)$ or $d(N)$ change in time.

The simplest extension of the above exponential growth is to make $d$ and $b$ linear in $N$ such that for a continous system we have the quadratic,

$$
\frac{dN}{dt} = rN - \lambda N^2
$$ {#eq-logistic}

where $r,\lambda > 0$ are constants. This continous ODE now has a population cap as small populations will grow and large populations shrink. It is easier to see this if we rewrite such that,
$$
\frac{dN}{dt} = r\left( 1 - \frac{N}{K} \right)N,\qquad \text{where} \quad K = \frac{r}{\lambda},
$$ {#eq-logisticRedef}
here $K$ is often refered to as a **carrying capacity**. This is called the **logistic equation**. It exhibits logarithmic solutions and we will study this system later in the course (both continous and discrete).

## Nondimensionalisation

In mathematical biology we are intrested in studying trends and comparing different models without focussing imediately on direct measurement. A useful way of abstracting our models so we can easily compare for example population models of bacteria and elephants on very different scales is **nondimensionalisation**, where we make variables (both dependent and independent) dimensionless. In general this will be the population N

In general this will involve rewriting the population and time as the dimensionless variables,
$$
n = \frac{N}{\tilde{N}}, \qquad \tau = \frac{t}{\tilde{T}}.
$${#eq-generalNonDim}
such that a general ODE transforms as,
$$
\frac{dN}{dt} = H(N(t)) \qquad \longrightarrow \qquad \frac{dn}{d\tau} = \frac{\tilde{T}}{\tilde{N}}\, H\left(  \right).
$$ {#eq-nonDimTransform}

A good example is the logistic equation in @eq-logisticRedef, where we absorb the constants by choosing $\tilde{N} = K$ and $\tilde{T} = 1/r$ such that we define,
$$
n = \frac{N}{K}, \qquad \tau = rt,
$$ {#eq-nonDim}
which we call the **dimensionless variables**. The equation then becomes significantly simpler,
$$
\frac{dn}{d\tau} = n(1-n).
$$ {#eq-nonDim}

So we have now stripped away all the parameters that are unnecessary for studying the features of behaviours of the model. It is easy to revert back to the original equation by simply substituting back in for $n$ and $\tau$.
 
Note, be careful with absorbing signs e.g. for @eq-continousExp, the exponential growth model, if we defined $\tau = r N$ we get the dimensionless solution,
$$
N(\tau) = N_0 \, e^{\tau}.
$$ {#eq-nonDimExp}
This may be suggestive that population always grows, but if $d > b \Leftrightarrow r < 0$ then the rescaling has reversed time.

### Dimensional analysis
The dimensions/units of each term in a model must be consistent. This observation helps to determine the units of different parameters in a model.

For example, we can deduce that the units of the parameter $r$ in @eq-expSol
$$
\frac{dN}{dt}=rN.
$$ {#eq-dim1}
The units of the left-hand term are 
$$
\frac{\# pop density}{\# time},
$$ {#eq-dim2}
thus the units of the right-hand side must match. This means that $r$ must have the units,
$$
\#r = \frac{1}{\#time},
$$ {#eq-dim3}
for dimensional consistency. This is a useful technique for making sure equations are correct and also gives some physical intuition as to what different parameters represent. In the above example $r$ is inverse in time, so it is describing a rate of change, which matches our intuiton that it is the difference in birth and death rate.
